subject: mathematics
question_text: Show that cot(π/16) · cot(2π/16) · cot(3π/16) · … · cot(7π/16) = 1.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.109 — from the book's separate "STAR QUESTIONS PLUS" bank, answer 172. That bank (book pp.98-111, answers 142-180) sits AFTER all the numbered chapters and is organised by chapter rather than forming part of any chapter's own inventory; it is authored into this unit because that is where the question belongs on the paper (founder decision 2026-08-22). SECTION: classed SAQ on its length and shape. The bank prints no mark cut, so this classification is OURS. Printed appearances: none — this answer carries no year tag. Seven factors, and they pair off from the two ends. Each outer pair multiplies to 1, and the middle factor cot(4π/16) = cot(π/4) is 1 on its own. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — the bank prints no [N Marks] tags anywhere. The shapes used follow the splits the book DOES print elsewhere: 1+1 for a 2-mark VSAQ (answers 100, 101 on book p.82), 1+1+1+1 or 1+2+1 for a 4-mark SAQ (answers 58, 59 on p.63 and 61 on p.64), and the granular split for a 7-mark LAQ (answer 32 on p.44). This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — name each move in order.

steps.label: Pair from the two ends
steps.margin_note: First mark. Write all seven factors, then bracket the first with the last, the second with the sixth, the third with the fifth — leaving the fourth alone.
steps.memory_tip: Write all seven factors, then bracket first with last, second with sixth, third with fifth — the fourth stands alone.

recall.must_convey: That the seven factors are paired from the two ends, leaving cot(4π/16) alone in the middle.
accept: pair the first with the last, the second with the sixth and the third with the fifth leaving the middle one alone
bracket the factors from the two ends inwards
there are seven factors so one is left in the middle
rendu ends nunchi pairs chesi middle one migilipoyindi

steps.why: Each pair sums to 8π/16 = π/2, which is what makes them complementary. Pairing from the ends is the only arrangement that does this.
common_mistakes: Losing the middle factor while bracketing.

steps.label: Rewrite each larger angle
steps.margin_note: Half the marks. In each pair the larger angle is π/2 minus the smaller — for example 7π/16 = (8π − π)/16 = π/2 − π/16.
steps.memory_tip: In each pair the larger angle is π/2 minus the smaller, and cot(π/2 − θ) = tan θ.

recall.must_convey: That each larger angle is written as π/2 minus the smaller, so cot of it becomes tan of the smaller, and cot(π/4) = 1.
accept: each larger angle is pi by two minus the smaller so its cotangent becomes the tangent of the smaller
seven pi by sixteen is pi by two minus pi by sixteen
cot of pi by two minus theta is tan theta, and the middle factor is cot pi by four which is one
peddha angle ni pi by two minus chinna ga rasthe cot tan avthundi
convert each larger angle to a complement

steps.why: Writing 8π/16 as the common numerator is what makes each complement visible. Working in degrees (90° − 11.25°) is the same move.
common_mistakes: Writing cot(π/2 − θ) as cot θ.

steps.label: Use cot θ · tan θ = 1
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Each bracket is a cotangent times its own tangent, which is 1 — so the product of three 1s and the middle 1 is 1.
steps.memory_tip: Each bracket is a cotangent times its OWN tangent, which is 1. The middle term cot(π/4) is 1 too.
lines: cot θ · tan θ = 1 for each pair.

recall.must_convey: That each pair gives cot θ · tan θ = 1, so the whole product is 1.
accept: cot theta times tan theta is one so every bracket is one and the product is one
the whole product comes to one
prathi pair one, so total one

steps.why: cot θ and tan θ are reciprocals, so their product is 1 for EVERY θ where both are defined — no particular angle is needed.
common_mistakes: Trying to evaluate each cotangent numerically.
Writing cot θ · tan θ as tan²θ.
